newsitem.title: USA: New talks to settle U.S.-Japan insurance dispute.
newsitem.headline: New talks to settle U.S.-Japan insurance dispute.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese trade negotiators began a new round of talks here Friday in hope of resolving a long-simmering dispute over how to open up Japan's giant insurance market.
U.S. Trade Representative Ira Shapiro and Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, led the negotiations, expected to run through Saturday.
The talks, which went into recess after about three hours and were due to be reconvened later Friday night, the chief negotiators told reporters.
They declined to comment on the progress of the discussions but Shapiro said the talks had so far been "useful".

At issue is Japan's $382 billion domestic insurance market. Washington is pressing Japan to liberalize its primary insurance markets before a niche area called the "Third Sector," where U.S. firms have been dominant, is opened up to Japanese insurers.
The Third Sector includes areas such as personal accident, illness and nursing care, such as stand-alone cancer policies.
Earlier Friday, Sakakibara told reporters that U.S. and Japanese negotiators were still looking for a way to resolve differences in opening up Japan's insurance market.

"Both sides are still searching (to see) how this can be resolved," Sakakibara said. He said the meeting was basically groundwork for further talks at the ministerial level, possibly at the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation forum meeting later this month.

Asked if Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's recently unveiled financial deregulation plan -- dubbed Big Bang after the 1986 British reforms -- would mandate a total liberalisation, Sakakibara said consistency was "an issue".
Before the talks began, a U.S. trade official involved in the negotiations said the United States would make "strong efforts" to reach an agreement at the San Francisco meeting.

"The United States is entering into these talks with the intention of making strong efforts to reach a resolution and we intend to work hard toward that goal," the U.S. official told Reuters. He spoke on the condition he not be identified.

The United States wants Japan to live up to a 1994 agreement that calls for deregulation of the primary sector dominated by big Japanese firms before deregulation of the so-called third sector of specialty insurance.

On Thursday, a U.S. trade official in Washington expressed doubt that the dispute would be fully resolved in these talks. The official said the "ball is substantially in Japan's court" because Tokyo removed a number of primary sector issues from the table during negotiations in September.

Little progress can be made if those issues are not returned to the table, the official said. He said a major sticking point for the United States is automobile insurance and pricing that would allow foreign firms to compete more effectively in the Japanese market.
The two sides have set a deadline of December 15 to resolve the issue, and Friday's talks were likely to go on late into the night.
On coming out of the first session, Shapiro said jokingly: "It's always a pleasure to get together on insurance."
